original.target_description: Study 1: full eligible USA sample; simple correlation between observer age and estimated age of the bistable woman.

n.sample_role: Final-sample participants contributing observer age and estimated woman age to the simple correlation.
n.exclusions: USA final sample after attention checks, valid demographic responses and estimated woman age older than 18 years; non-USA respondents excluded. Recruitment: 666 overall, 418 USA; final USA sample 393.

replication.target_description: Study 1: full eligible sample; one-tailed Pearson correlation between participant age and estimated age of ambiguous figure.

n.exclusions: 14 of 260 recruited participants excluded following eligibility checks (person and female identification), leaving 246.
n.location: Methods, Participants, first paragraph (publisher full-text HTML)
n.quote: An analysis of participants’ eligibility for inclusion (see below for criteria) resulted in the exclusion of 14 participants, reducing the final sample to N = 246.

es.location: Results, Primary analyses: replication of original findings (canonical HTML text; PDF pagination unavailable)
es.quote:
A one-tailed Pearson correlation was computed between participants’ own-age and their age estimates of the ambiguous figure. Results indicated that there was a significant positive association between participants’ age and their age estimates;
r
(244) = 0.22,
p
< 0.001

reported_success.location: p. 4, Results, Primary analyses: replication of original findings, first paragraph (publisher full-text HTML)
reported_success.quote: Similar results were obtained in the original experiment of Nicholls et al., who found a mean age difference of 6.32 years and a correlation of 0.24.

notes:
Extracted the full-sample correlation, not the percept-specific or unfamiliar-only correlations. Original prints r(393); analytic n is independently documented as 393. The replication reproduces the age-estimate relationship while disputing its interpretation as a perceptual bias.
